podcast.title: Dave Farrell's Temporary Departure (1999)
podcast.body: Bass player Dave Farrell left Hybrid Theory in 1999 to tour the Christian circuit with his previous band, Tasty Snacks, which further complicated the band's efforts to secure a record deal at a critical juncture. "Didn't help that Dave, the bass player, left a tour of the Christian circuit with Tasty Snacks that year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dozens of Record Label Rejections (1999)
podcast.body: After forming and changing their name from Zero to Hybrid Theory, the band faced "dozens" of rejections from both major and independent labels in 1999. Chester Bennington recalled performing at nearly 50 showcases without attracting any interest or offers. "In fact, they were turned down dozens of times in 1999 by both major labels and indie labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dozens of Record Label Rejections (1999)
podcast.body: Hybrid Theory faced significant challenges in securing a record deal, being turned down by record labels at least 42 times, which was explicitly stated as not an exaggeration. "The third theory was turned down by record labels at least 42 times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Internet Promotion
podcast.body: Hybrid Theory was an early adopter of internet-based self-promotion, establishing an online street team consisting of volunteers. These volunteers engaged in various chat rooms and music forums to publicize the band's record, although this strategy initially did not lead to widespread success. "They must have been one of the first bands to properly use the internet to publicize themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mandatory Name Change to Linkin Park
podcast.body: The band was forced to change their name from Hybrid Theory in 1999 to avoid legal issues, as another band with the same name already existed in Wales and was signed to Warner Brothers Records. This legal necessity led to the adoption of the name Linkin Park. "they really didn't have much choice because it turned out that there was already a band in Wales called Hybrid Theory, so they had to change their name to avoid any messy legal situations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Change from Zero
podcast.body: After Chester Bennington joined the band, Zero changed its name to Hybrid Theory. "The band changed their name to Hybrid Theory and they recorded a self-titled EP."

podcast.title: Rejected Band Names
podcast.body: Before settling on Linkin Park, the group considered other names such as "Clear" (as in transparent), "Probing Loggers," and "Platinum Lotus Foundation." "The group went through a bunch of possibilities, clear as in transparent, probing loggers. No. Platinum Lotus Foundation."

xref.title: Chester Bennington's Former Band
xref.body: Before relocating to Los Angeles and joining Zero/Hybrid Theory, Chester Bennington was the singer for a band called Grey Days in Phoenix. He left the group due to internal disagreements. "While in Phoenix, Chester became the singer of a band called Grey Days, but there were disagreements and Chester decided to move to LA"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dave Farrell's Previous Band
xref.body: Tasty Snacks was a Christian Scott punk band that Dave "Phoenix" Farrell was a member of. He temporarily left Hybrid Theory in 1999 to tour the Christian circuit with them. "A former member of a Christian Scott punk band called Tasty Snacks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Phoenix Bands
xref.body: Before moving to Los Angeles to audition for Hybrid Theory (which became Linkin Park), Chester Bennington was active in the Phoenix music scene. Around age 17 in 1993, he sang in a band with his friend Sean, initially "Sean Dattel and his friends?" and then co-formed Gray Daze, which existed from late 1993 through 1998. "We now turn our attention to the parts that came together to form Lincoln Park, specifically what Chester Bennington was up to in Phoenix before he was invited to move to LA to sing for this new group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Success Amidst Piracy
xref.body: Despite the "all-time peak" of illegal file sharing platforms like Napster, LimeWire, and Kazaa when their first two albums were released, Linkin Park achieved immense commercial success, selling a combined 57 million copies worldwide from Hybrid Theory and Meteora. "But for God's sake, 57 million in sales from just two albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Gray Daze Frustration
xref.body: Despite Gray Daze being a local sensation in Phoenix, releasing two indie albums ("Wake Me" in 1994 and "No Sun Today" in 1997) and opening for international acts, they failed to attract major record labels. Burned out and discouraged, Chester quit the group in 1998, contemplating giving up music altogether, until he received the call to audition for Hybrid Theory. "So burned out and discouraged, Chester quit the group in 1998, and thought about giving up music called together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Intense Touring Schedule
xref.body: In the year immediately following the release of their debut album, Hybrid Theory, Linkin Park demonstrated an extraordinary work ethic by performing 320 shows. "In the first year after hybrid theory came out, they played 320 shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Japanese Special Edition of Hybrid Theory
xref.body: A unique two-disc version of Linkin Park's debut album, Hybrid Theory, was sold in Japan. The first disc contained the standard album, while the second disc featured a collection of unreleased live tracks and additional studio recordings. "there was a special two-disc version of hybrid theory sold in Japan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Most Pirated Rock Artist
xref.body: Linkin Park was identified as the most pirated rock act of the 2000s, with their music, particularly from the *Hybrid Theory* album, being widely shared illegally. "No one had their music pirated more apparently than Lincoln Park."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Change from Hybrid Theory
xref.body: The band changed its name to "Linkin Park" from "Hybrid Theory" after being inspired by an actual park of the same name in Santa Monica that they drove by daily. They believed it to be a universally recognizable name, as many American towns reportedly have a Lincoln Park. "Hybrid Theory became the deliberately misspelled Lincoln Park."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer of Hybrid Theory
xref.body: Don Gilmore produced Linkin Park's debut album, Hybrid Theory. His demanding approach in the studio caused significant tension with the band, particularly with Chester Bennington. "He was driving them nuts with the way he was pushing them in the studio."

xref.title: Temporary Departure from Hybrid Theory
xref.body: In 1999, Farrell temporarily left Hybrid Theory to tour the Christian circuit with his former band, Tasty Snacks. This absence necessitated the hiring of two session bass players for Linkin Park's debut album, *Hybrid Theory*, with Brad Delson filling in for any unplayed parts. "Didn't help that Dave, the bass player, left a tour of the Christian circuit with Tasty Snacks that year."
